title: Area III review: Airport Operations
intro: These questions mix both Tasks of Area III: radio calls, light signals and airport lighting, plus traffic patterns. Most put you in one commercial flight where you need both Tasks at once, from charter departures to no-radio arrivals.

questions.q: You arrive at night at Ridgeview just after its part-time tower has closed. The sectional shows a star by the tower frequency and "RP 23" in the airport data. You will land on Runway 23. What is your plan for the radio, the lights and the pattern?
options: Call the tower frequency and ask the controller to turn the runway lights up, then fly right traffic for Runway 23
Key the mike 3 times first so the lights don't blind you, and fly whichever pattern direction suits you
Self-announce on the CTAF, key the mike 7 times on the lighting frequency, and fly left traffic, because RP notes apply only while the tower is open
Self-announce on the CTAF, key the mike 7 times on the lighting frequency from the Chart Supplement, and fly right traffic for Runway 23
questions.why: With the tower closed and no FSS, you self-announce on the CTAF [[33:209|AIM 4-1-9g2]]. Radio control of lighting is often available when a part-time tower is closed [[33:129|AIM 2-1-8]]. Key 7 times first for full intensity, then adjust down, and get the frequency from the Chart Supplement or approach chart, because the sectional does not show it [[33:132|AIM 2-1-8c-d]]. "RP 23" means a right pattern on Runway 23 [[17:4|AC 90-66C 8.2.1.1]]. The tempting "left traffic" answer is wrong: a closed tower does not cancel the pattern shown on the chart, and the flow rules still apply when a towered airport is operating as a non-towered one [[17:4|AC 90-66C 8.2.1.1]]. Asking the tower fails because the tower controls the lights, and a closed tower cannot [[33:129|AIM 2-1-7]].

questions.q: On a 5-mile final at a non-towered airport, you are flying a practice RNAV approach to Runway 9 and plan to circle to Runway 27, which has right traffic. A Cessna is in the pattern. Which plan follows the guidance?
options: Announce "JAWBO inbound, RNAV 9" and circle to the left, since circling approaches always use left turns
Announce "5 miles west, inbound RNAV Runway 9, circling Runway 27," coordinate with the Cessna, and circle to the right
Announce your fix names on the CTAF so instrument pilots know where you are, then circle to the right
Fly straight in to Runway 9 against the flow, since IFR traffic has priority over the Cessna
questions.why: A non-instrument pilot may not know where your fixes are, so give direction and distance from the airport plus your intentions [[17:9|AC 90-66C 9.11.5]] [[17:10|AC 90-66C 9.11.5]]. Final for Runway 9 lies west of the airport, since you fly east to land. If the Chart Supplement lists right traffic, practice approaches in VMC circle to the right, and IFR traffic has no priority over VFR traffic [[17:9|AC 90-66C 9.11.3]]. After you coordinate with the pattern traffic, breaking off to join downwind may be safest [[17:9|AC 90-66C 9.11.4.2]]. The fix-name answer has the right turn direction but the wrong call.

questions.q: In daylight your radio dies just outside a Class D airport. The weather is VFR. You stay clear until you learn the traffic flow, join the pattern, and on final the tower gives you a steady green. The PAPI shows one white and three red. What now?
options: You are cleared to land; add power and pitch to get back to two white and two red, and stay at or above that glide path
Go around, because a no-radio airplane needs a flashing green before it may land
Continue as you are, since the glide path rule applies only to large and turbine-powered airplanes
Steady green means return for landing, so fly another pattern and wait for the next signal
questions.why: With a VFR radio failure you may land in Class D with basic VFR weather, visual contact with the tower and a clearance to land [[60:453|14 CFR 91.129(d)(2)]], and a steady green in flight is that clearance [[60:451|14 CFR 91.125]]. One white and three red is slightly low [[33:124|AIM FIG 2-1-5]]. In Class D any airplane landing on a runway with a visual approach slope indicator must stay at or above the glide path until lower is needed for a safe landing [[60:453|14 CFR 91.129(e)(3)]]. Add power and pitch together to shallow the descent [[24:175|AFH 9-4]]. The tempting "large and turbine only" answer mixes up paragraph (e)(1), the 1,500-foot entry rule, with (e)(3), which covers every airplane [[60:453|14 CFR 91.129(e)]]. Flashing green, not steady green, means return for landing [[60:451|14 CFR 91.125]].

questions.q: You fly a single-engine turboprop for a charter company out of a Class D airport at 640 feet MSL. No departure procedure or cloud clearance gets in the way. Which of these is a regulation for you there, not just a recommendation?
options: Fly the pattern at 1,640 feet MSL, the same as the piston traffic
Cross midfield at 2,640 feet MSL before an entry from the upwind side
Leave the pattern with a 45 degree turn after reaching pattern altitude
After takeoff, climb to 2,140 feet MSL as rapidly as practicable
questions.why: In Class D, each pilot of a turbine-powered airplane must climb to 1,500 feet above the surface as rapidly as practicable [[60:454|14 CFR 91.129(g)(2)]]: 640 + 1,500 = 2,140 feet MSL. You must also enter the pattern at least 1,500 feet above the airport (2,140 feet MSL), so 1,640 feet MSL (640 + 1,000) is too low for you [[60:453|14 CFR 91.129(e)(1)]]. The 2,000-foot AGL midfield crossing (640 + 2,000 = 2,640) is AFH advice for airports where turbine aircraft operate, not a rule [[24:168|AFH 8-4]], and the 45 degree departure turn is a recommended practice [[17:15|AC 90-66C 11.8]].

questions.q: At night you fly VFR over rising terrain, getting advisories from Approach with your Mode C transponder on. You want the controller's automatic low-altitude warning to watch your flight. What do you do, and how do you treat an alert if one comes?
options: Nothing, because MSAW monitors every VFR aircraft that has a Mode C transponder
Ask for MSAW monitoring. If an alert comes, check your altitude at once; what to do about it is your decision
Squawk 7700 so MSAW will track you, and fly the controller's vector out of the area
Ask for MSAW monitoring. If an alert comes, the controller takes over terrain clearance and you must fly the vector
questions.why: MSAW watches IFR aircraft automatically, but a VFR aircraft with Mode C is monitored only if the pilot asks: "request MSAW monitoring" [[33:217|AIM 4-1-16a2]]. A safety alert warns of unsafe closeness to terrain, obstructions or other aircraft, and once it is issued, what to do is solely the pilot's prerogative [[33:216|AIM 4-1-16]]. Vectors are advice only, and flying safely stays your job [[33:217|AIM 4-1-17b]]. 7700 is the emergency code, not a way to get MSAW [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2a2]].

questions.q: You are IFR in a charter Baron at a non-towered airport. ATC has released you with a void time two minutes away. As you hold short of Runway 18, a Cessna calls a 2-mile final to Runway 36. What is the best action?
options: Take off at once; the IFR release is your takeoff clearance and the void time is close
Take off now, because IFR traffic has priority over a VFR airplane on final
Announce on the CTAF and make sure no one is on short final first; if it is not clear, skip the departure, even if the void time passes
Say "taking the runway" on the CTAF and go, since a Cessna 2 miles out has time to land after you
questions.why: An IFR clearance or the word "released" is not authority to take off at a non-towered airport; announce on the CTAF and make sure no one is on short final before you go [[17:14|AC 90-66C 10.4.4]]. Check for landing traffic aligned with your runway or landing toward you [[17:6|AC 90-66C 9.5.1]]: a Cessna landing on Runway 36 would meet your Runway 18 takeoff head-on. Don't accept an immediate departure just to meet a void time [[17:14|AC 90-66C 10.4.4]]. An aircraft on final approach has the right-of-way over aircraft in flight or on the surface [[60:448|14 CFR 91.113(g)]].

questions.q: At night both your radios are dead, and you have joined the pattern at a Class D airport. The tower aims a flashing green light at you. What does it mean, and how do you answer?
options: Cleared to land; rock your wings
Return for landing, with a steady green to follow; blink your landing or navigation lights
Airport unsafe, do not land; blink your landing or navigation lights
Cleared to taxi; move the ailerons or rudder
questions.why: In flight, a flashing green means return for landing, to be followed by a steady green at the proper time [[60:451|14 CFR 91.125]]. At night you acknowledge by blinking the landing or navigation lights; rocking the wings is the daytime answer [[33:235|AIM 4-2-13a2]]. "Cleared to land" is the steady green. "Airport unsafe" is the flashing red. "Cleared to taxi" is what flashing green means for an aircraft on the surface, where the daytime answer is moving the ailerons or rudder [[33:257|AIM 4-3-13e]].

questions.q: You land behind a business jet that touched down about 1,200 feet beyond the threshold bar of Runway 27, which has a 900-foot displaced threshold. Where should you plan to touch down?
options: In the 900-foot displaced area, to get the most runway ahead of you
Just past the threshold bar, 300 feet in, well before the jet's touchdown point
Beyond the point where the jet touched down, more than 1,200 feet past the threshold bar
Anywhere past the threshold bar, since the jet's wake ended when it slowed down
questions.why: Landing behind a larger aircraft on the same runway, stay at or above its final approach path, note its touchdown point and land beyond it [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6b1]], because its wake ends at touchdown [[34:148|AIM 7-4-4a]]. The runway behind a displaced threshold is available for takeoffs either way and for landings only from the opposite direction, so you may not land there on Runway 27 [[33:141|AIM 2-3-3h2]]. Landing short of the jet's touchdown point puts you in the wake it left on final.

questions.q: You are taxiing out at an airport with Runway Status Lights. To keep the ground radar screen clear, your passenger suggests leaving the transponder in STBY until you take the runway, as "Lights, Camera, Action" says. What is right?
options: Leave it in STBY until cleared for takeoff, then turn it on
Turn it on only if the tower asks you to squawk
Leave it in STBY on the ground; RWSL works from the tower's clearances, not from your transponder
Turn on altitude reporting and ADS-B Out when you leave parking, and leave them on until you shut down at parking
questions.why: At RWSL airports, operate with the transponder and ADS-B on from leaving the parking area until shutdown at parking, so the surveillance systems that drive RWSL can see you [[33:129|AIM 2-1-6d1]]. At all airports, use altitude reporting and ADS-B Out anywhere on the movement area [[33:221|AIM 4-1-20a3]]. "Lights, Camera, Action" is a final check when cleared for takeoff or before taking the runway, not the first time to turn the transponder on [[16:10|AC 90-48E 10.4.1]]. RWSL is fully automatic and works from surveillance data, not from clearances [[33:127|AIM 2-1-6a]].

questions.q: On a charter flight, a passenger becomes ill and needs a doctor soon, but is stable, and the airplane is fine. You are talking to Approach on an assigned code, 30 miles from a towered airport. What is the best call?
options: Say "MAYDAY" three times, then squawk 7700 and give your position and intentions
Wait until you reach the tower, since a sick passenger who is stable is not an emergency
Squawk 7700 first, then call on 121.5 and ask for a doctor on the ground
Say "PAN-PAN" three times, then your call sign, the problem and your intentions, keeping your assigned code
questions.why: This is an urgency condition: a safety concern needing timely help. Use PAN-PAN, preferably three times; it has priority over all communications except distress [[34:45|AIM 6-3-1c-d]]. In contact with ATC, keep your assigned code; 7700 is for when you can't make contact right away [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2a2]]. Then give the message elements in order [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2a3]]. MAYDAY is for grave and imminent danger. Waiting is the classic error: ask for help early, not after it becomes distress [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2a]].

questions.q: At a towered airport you are on short final for Runway 27 when the tower says, "Bonanza Four Kilo X-ray, Runway 27, cleared to land, caution wake turbulence, Citation departing ahead." You see the Citation rotate about 3,000 feet down the 5,000-foot runway. Where should you plan to touch down?
options: Near the far end of the runway, so you stay above the Citation's climb path
Beyond the 3,000-foot mark, since its wake ends where it lifts off
Well before the 3,000-foot mark where the Citation rotated
Anywhere, since wake turbulence matters only behind a landing aircraft
questions.why: Landing behind a departing larger aircraft on the same runway, note its rotation point and land well before it [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6b4]]. A wake begins when the aircraft rotates [[34:148|AIM 7-4-4a]], so the vortices lie from the 3,000-foot mark onward, and touching down beyond that point puts you in them. Staying above the larger aircraft's path and landing beyond its touchdown point is the advice behind a landing aircraft, not behind a departure [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6b1]]. Even with the caution, the pilot is expected to adjust the flight path to avoid a serious wake encounter [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6a]].

questions.q: On short final behind a business jet, you hit its wake. The airplane rolls, and a wingtip scrapes the runway as you land. No one is hurt, and only the wingtip is damaged. What does 49 CFR 830 require, and what was the wake lesson?
options: Notify the NTSB immediately, since any wake upset counts as a flight control system malfunction
File an NTSB report within 10 days, since any damage to the aircraft makes it an accident
No NTSB notice is required, since wingtip damage is not substantial damage; next time land before the jet's touchdown point
No NTSB notice is required, since wingtip damage is not substantial damage; next time stay at or above the jet's path and land beyond its touchdown point
questions.why: An accident needs death, serious injury or substantial damage [[60:881|49 CFR 830.2]]. Damage to wingtips is specifically not substantial damage [[60:882|49 CFR 830.2]]. A wake upset is not on the immediate-notice list of serious incidents, which covers things like a flight control system malfunction or failure, an in-flight fire or an in-flight collision [[60:882|49 CFR 830.5(a)]]. The controls worked, so the malfunction answer is wrong. To avoid the wake, stay at or above the larger aircraft's path and land beyond its touchdown point [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6b1]].

questions.q: You taxi a charter Cessna toward Runway 36 at a non-towered airport and come to a marking of four yellow lines, two solid and two dashed. Where do you stop, and what do you do before crossing?
options: Stop with the solid lines nearest you; announce on the CTAF and check for landing traffic before you cross
Stop with the dashed lines nearest you; cross when the CTAF is quiet
Stop with the solid lines nearest you and wait for the tower to clear you across
Roll across; the marking binds you only at airports with an operating tower
questions.why: The solid lines are always on the side where the aircraft must hold [[33:151|AIM 2-3-5a]]. At an airport without an operating tower, you must make sure you have adequate separation from other aircraft before crossing the marking [[33:151|AIM 2-3-5a1]]. Announce your runway and direction of flight on the CTAF, and do not enter the runway until you have checked for landing traffic aligned with it or landing toward you [[17:6|AC 90-66C 9.5.3]] [[17:6|AC 90-66C 9.5.1]]. Waiting for a tower clearance is the towered-airport rule, and a quiet CTAF is not proof of an empty pattern [[17:10|AC 90-66C 9.12.2]].

questions.q: On a VFR final at a non-towered airport you pass 400 feet AGL with the PAPI showing four white lights. Your groundspeed is 80 knots and the touchdown zone is 2,400 feet ahead. About what descent rate would it take to land there, and what do you do?
options: About 1,350 fpm, beyond the 500 to 1,000 fpm of a stabilized approach, so go around
About 1,350 fpm; push over to it, since being above the glide path is always legal
About 425 fpm, the normal 3 degree rate, so continue and land long
About 1,350 fpm; slow well below landing speed to steepen the descent, then land
questions.why: Four white means high, more than 3.5 degrees [[33:124|AIM FIG 2-1-5]]. At 80 knots you cover about 135 feet per second (80 × 6,076 ÷ 3,600), so 2,400 feet takes about 17.8 seconds, and 400 ÷ 17.8 × 60 = about 1,350 fpm, a 9.5 degree path. A stabilized approach uses generally 500 to 1,000 fpm, with a +10/-5 knot speed window, and pilots typically go around if they are not stabilized by 500 feet above the airport in VMC [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]. A 3 degree path at 80 knots is only about 425 fpm. Staying above the glide path is what the Class D VASI rule asks [[60:453|14 CFR 91.129(e)(3)]], but legal does not mean stable. Slowing below the landing speed breaks the airspeed window [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

questions.q: IFR in a complex single, your radios fail in VMC 30 miles from your destination, a Class D airport where the weather is good VFR. What is the best plan?
options: Keep flying the 91.185(c) route and altitude, and start the approach at your ETA
Land at the nearest strip you can reach, even a short one, because "practicable" means "possible"
Continue VFR and land as soon as practicable: squawk 7600, stay outside or above the Class D surface area until you know the traffic flow, join the pattern and land on a steady green
Fly straight in to the Class D airport, since an IFR flight plan needs no landing clearance after a radio failure
questions.why: If the failure occurs in VFR conditions, continue under VFR and land as soon as practicable [[60:482|14 CFR 91.185(b)]]. "Practicable" is not "possible": you don't have to use an unsuitable airport or land minutes short of your destination [[34:53|AIM 6-4-1c2]]. Squawk 7600 [[34:54|AIM 6-4-2]], then follow the no-radio arrival: remain outside or above the surface area until you know the flow, join the pattern and watch for light signals [[33:235|AIM 4-2-13a3]]. Landing in Class D still needs a clearance, which can be a steady green [[60:453|14 CFR 91.129(d)(2)]] [[60:451|14 CFR 91.125]]. The 91.185(c) route and altitude are for failures in IFR conditions [[60:482|14 CFR 91.185(c)]].

questions.q: No radio information is available as you overfly a non-towered airport with Runways 9 and 27. The wind sock hangs limp. The small end of the tetrahedron points west, and the traffic pattern indicators show right traffic for Runway 27. You hear and see no other traffic. What is the best plan?
options: Land Runway 9, because the small end of the tetrahedron points into the wind
Land Runway 27 with left traffic, because left turns are always standard
Skip the pattern and fly a straight-in to either runway, since no one else is around
Expect Runway 27, but use extreme caution with the tetrahedron in calm wind; if you land there, fly the right traffic the indicators show
questions.why: The small end of a tetrahedron points in the direction of landing, so pointing west means Runway 27. In very light or calm wind, use extreme caution, because it may not match the calm-wind runway [[33:244|AIM 4-3-4b3]]. When approaching to land, all turns are to the left unless a traffic pattern indicator shows right turns [[33:244|AIM 4-3-4c]] [[60:451|14 CFR 91.126(b)]]. Check the indicators from above pattern altitude, then fly well clear before descending to enter [[17:14|AC 90-66C 11.2]]. Some aircraft have no radio, so silence doesn't mean an empty pattern [[17:10|AC 90-66C 9.12.2]], and the FAA discourages VFR straight-ins [[33:209|AIM 4-1-9g4]].

questions.q: At night on downwind at a non-towered airport, you catch a faint light ahead and to the right, but when you look straight at it, it seems to fade. What is the best technique?
options: Look about 10 degrees to one side of it and scan the area around it
Stare at it harder until it comes back
Turn off your landing light and strobes so your eyes can adjust
Assume it is a ground light, since any aircraft in the pattern would call on the CTAF
questions.why: Night scanning depends almost entirely on peripheral vision, because the night blind spot, 5 to 10 degrees wide, sits in the center of your view. Look about 10 degrees off to one side of a dim object and scan around it, with short stops of a few seconds [[16:13|AC 90-48E 13.1]]. Some aircraft have no radio, so a quiet CTAF does not mean an empty pattern [[17:10|AC 90-66C 9.12.2]]. Keep your own lights on so others can see you [[33:266|AIM 4-3-24c]].

questions.q: On the tower frequency you hear another pilot say, "Tower, Mooney Two Three Papa, ten south, landing, with the numbers." The airport has ATIS. What has that pilot told the tower?
options: That he has only the wind, runway and altimeter, and not the ATIS
That he has the ATIS and the weather from the ASOS
That he has the runway assignment and a landing clearance
That he has the current ATIS, so the controller can skip everything in it
questions.why: "Have numbers" means you have received the wind, runway and altimeter ONLY. It does not mean you have the ATIS and should never be used for that [[33:213|AIM 4-1-13h]]. The right way is to repeat the ATIS code letter on initial contact, such as "information Sierra received" [[33:213|AIM 4-1-13d]]. Then the controller may omit current items in the broadcast [[33:213|AIM 4-1-13e]]. Without the code, the controller has to give that pilot the pertinent information [[33:213|AIM 4-1-13f]]. Nothing in the call is a landing clearance; you still need one from the tower [[60:454|14 CFR 91.129(i)]].

questions.q: After takeoff you are squawking 2600 when Approach says, "Squawk 7210." Which way of changing the dial avoids a false alarm at ATC?
questions.why: While changing codes, avoid selecting 7500, 7600 to 7677 or 7700 to 7777, because they trigger alarms at automated ground facilities [[33:223|AIM 4-1-20e1]]. Changing the first digit first would put 7600 (lost radio), 7700 (emergency) or 7610 on the dial on the way. Changing the middle digits first gives 2210, which is safe, and then 7210 [[33:223|AIM 4-1-20e1]]. The AIM's own example does the same: from 2700 to 7200, go through 2200, not 7700.

questions.q: After a night landing you exit on a taxiway whose centerline lights alternate green and yellow. The tower tells you to contact Ground. Where may you stop?
options: As soon as the airplane is off the runway pavement
Only after you pass the alternating green and yellow lights, since until then you are still within the runway environment or ILS critical area
At the first yellow light, which marks the hold line
Anywhere on the taxiway, since green and yellow lights are only for low visibility
questions.why: Lead-off lights alternate green and yellow from the runway centerline to one light beyond the runway holding position or ILS critical area holding position. The color code warns you that you are still within the runway environment or ILS critical area [[33:126|AIM 2-1-5c]]. An exiting aircraft is not clear of the runway until all parts have crossed the holding position marking [[33:151|AIM 2-3-5a1]]. Being off the pavement edge is not the same as being clear. Taxiway centerline lights beyond that point are steady green [[33:133|AIM 2-1-10b]].

questions.q: In daylight your radio quits on the ramp at a towered airport. You phone the tower and get approval to depart without two-way radio. At the hold line you get a steady green. How do you acknowledge, and what does it mean?
options: Rock your wings; it means cleared to taxi onto the runway and hold
Blink the landing light; it means return to the starting point
Move the ailerons or rudder; it means cleared for takeoff
Move the ailerons or rudder; it means cleared to taxi
questions.why: If the radio fails before you leave parking and can't be fixed, phone the tower for authorization to depart without two-way radio. On the ground in daylight, acknowledge light signals by moving the ailerons or rudder [[33:235|AIM 4-2-13b]]. A steady green to an aircraft on the surface means cleared for takeoff; flashing green means cleared to taxi, and flashing white means return to starting point [[60:451|14 CFR 91.125]]. Rocking the wings is the in-flight acknowledgment [[33:235|AIM 4-2-13a2]].
